extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, IP professionals, in-house counsel and patent proprietors concerned with EPO filings and prior-art practice
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing whether commercially available products and associated technical information constitute prior art under Article 54(2) EPC following the EPO Enlarged Board decision G 1/23. Useful for advising on novelty, inventive step, and filing strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility is not a legal requirement for prior art status
rubrics_metrics.description: The Enlarged Board has clarified that reproducibility is not a legal requirement for prior art status under the EPC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A product should not be excluded from the state of the art merely because it cannot be analysed and reproduced without undue burden; public availability (factual accessibility) is the determinative criterion. The Board rejected reading G 1/92 as imposing an enablement/reproducibility test for Article 54(2) EPC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public availability / factual accessibility determines state of the art
rubrics_metrics.description: What matters under Article 54(2) EPC is whether the product or information was factually accessible to the public, not whether it was fully analysable or reproducible by the skilled person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the product or information was made publicly accessible (e.g., marketed, exhibited, published) — if so, it forms part of the state of the art regardless of reproducibility. Focus enquiries on actual accessibility evidence (sales, brochures, datasheets, catalogue circulation, public demonstrations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial products are prior art from the moment they are marketed
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial products are prior art as soon as they are marketed, with no second chance to patent them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent practitioners must treat any commercial availability (sale, offer for sale, public distribution) before filing as destroying novelty under Article 54(2) EPC. This has practical effect similar to the US 'on-sale bar'—public offering of the product can prevent later patenting even by the original producer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical information in brochures, datasheets and literature counts as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical information about such a product (e.g. in brochures or literature) is also part of the state of the art, regardless of reproducibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate marketing materials, datasheets, manuals and other public documentation for technical disclosures. Even if the internal composition or manufacture cannot be reproduced, features disclosed in such materials are prior art that can be relied on for novelty and inventive step attacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of inventive step depends on derivable technical teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: While non-reproducible products cannot be excluded from prior art status under Article 54(2) EPC, the extent to which such products contribute to the assessment of inventive step depends on what technical teaching the skilled person can actually derive from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using a marketed product as prior art for inventive step, consider what a skilled person could plausibly learn: the product's analysable properties, standard analytical results, the skilled person's common general knowledge, and any practical limitations. The contribution to inventive step is context-dependent and may be limited if little technical teaching can be extracted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of 'reproduce' construed as reproduce 'by a different route'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board interpreted 'reproduce' in the referred questions as meaning reproduction 'by a different route', i.e. manufacturing from different starting materials rather than simply obtaining the product from the market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between acquiring the product (purchasing the marketed item) and reproducing it via independent manufacture. The decision treats factual availability of the marketed product as determinative; inability to manufacture the same product by a different route does not exclude the marketed product from prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: G 1/92 'analysis without undue burden' condition left open
rubrics_metrics.description: Since reproducibility is not required, the Board noted it was unnecessary to further interpret the 'analysis without undue burden' requirement condition from G 1/92, leaving this open for future clarification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume a clarified standard for 'analysis without undue burden' will be applied yet; be cautious when relying on or arguing against analysis/enabling-based exclusions until further case law or guidance is issued. Preserve factual records about analysability in proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard analytical identification of features makes those features prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Features that can be identified through standard analysis of a marketed product, or are disclosed in brochures, datasheets, or other technical materials, form part of the state of the art, regardless of whether the product itself is reproducible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing novelty/inventive step, include any features reasonably identifiable by usual analytical techniques. Collect and present analytical evidence (e.g., composition analysis, performance data) when relying on or defending against such prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical filing guidance: early filing is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision reinforces the importance of securing patent protection before making a product publicly available, including by sale or disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt filing strategies to file before launches, public demonstrations or distribution; consider confidentiality measures prior to filing. This is especially critical in polymers, pharmaceuticals, advanced materials and other fields where products may not be easily reverse engineered yet still become prior art when marketed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility-based exclusions lead to absurd outcomes and are therefore unreliable
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board found that interpreting G 1/92 as imposing a reproducibility requirement leads to legally untenable outcomes and lacks support under the EPC; strict reproducibility requirements would logically render virtually all materials unavailable as prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments that seek to exclude marketed products from prior art on the basis that essential starting materials or exact manufacture methods are non-reproducible face a strong headwind post-G 1/23. Counsel should prepare alternative lines of defence or attack that focus on factual accessibility and the actual technical teaching derivable from the product.
